title: Chemical measurements, conservation of mass and the quantitative interpretation of chemical equations
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank for AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) (review status in the bank: authored-gated-unreviewed). Terms: 4.3.1-c14, 4.3.1-c10, 4.3.1-c15, 4.3.1-c13. Clues: 4.3.1-c14 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.3.1-c10 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.3.1-c15 first sentence of the bank's definition; 4.3.1-c13 first sentence of the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Distribution of results
items.clue: The pattern formed by a set of repeated measurements, showing where the results cluster and which of them lie apart from the rest.

items.label: Non-enclosed system
items.clue: A reaction vessel open to the surroundings, so a gaseous reactant can enter or a gaseous product can leave without being weighed on the balance.

items.label: Anomalous result
items.clue: A measurement lying well outside the cluster formed by the others; it is spotted when the distribution is represented and is excluded from the mean.

items.label: Uncertainty
items.clue: The doubt that always exists about the result of a measurement, present whenever a measurement is made, however good the apparatus and the technique.

questions.stem: A weighed piece of copper is heated in an open crucible. The mass of the solid increases. Why?

options.text: Oxygen from the air has combined with the copper to form copper oxide.
Heat energy absorbed from the flame has added to the mass of the metal.
The copper atoms expand as they get hot, so each one becomes much heavier.
New copper atoms are made as the reaction goes on in the crucible.

questions.explanation: 2Cu + O2 -> 2CuO. The oxide is heavier than the metal because the oxygen taken from the air is now weighed with it.

questions.stem: A student reads 25.00 cm3 from a burette, working carefully. Which statement about that measurement is correct?

options.text: There is always some uncertainty about the result, however careful you are.
There is no uncertainty, because a burette is precise apparatus.
Uncertainty appears only if the student misreads the burette scale.
Uncertainty would disappear if the whole titration were repeated three times.

questions.explanation: Whenever a measurement is made there is always some uncertainty about the result obtained.

questions.stem: Copper carbonate is heated in an open test tube: CuCO3 -> CuO + CO2. The mass of the solid falls. Why?

options.text: Some of the solid has been burned away by the heat of the Bunsen flame.
Carbon dioxide escapes, leaving copper oxide as the solid.
Mass is lost from the tube, so mass is not conserved in this reaction.
Strong heating has destroyed some of the solid, so that part no longer exists.

questions.explanation: In the thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate the carbon dioxide escapes into the atmosphere, leaving the metal oxide as the only solid product.

questions.stem: Five titres are 24.8, 25.0, 25.1, 25.0 and 27.4 cm3. How should this set of results be handled?

options.text: Include all five in the mean, because a measured result may never be dropped.
Plot all five, treat 27.4 as anomalous and leave it out of the mean.
Just take the mean and treat it as the exact result, since averaging removes any doubt.
Use a single titre, since a precise burette gives the exact volume.

questions.explanation: Representing the distribution shows 27.4 lying well away from the cluster, which is how an anomaly is identified.

questions.stem: Use the particle model to explain why the balance reading falls when a metal carbonate is heated in an open tube.

options.text: The particles left in the tube move further apart, so the solid weighs less than before.
Gas particles carry no mass of their own, so the reading falls as gas forms.
Particles are destroyed as the solid turns into a gas inside the hot tube.
Carbon dioxide particles leave the tube and mix into the air, so they are no longer weighed.

questions.stem: Four titres have a mean of 25.0 cm3, a lowest value of 24.8 cm3 and a highest of 25.2 cm3. How should the result be quoted?

options.text: 25.0 plus or minus 0.4 cm3, quoting the whole range as the uncertainty.
Report all four titres separately, since no reading may be left out.
25.0 plus or minus 0.2 cm3, which is half the range of 0.4 cm3.
25.0 cm3 exactly, since averaging the titres removes the uncertainty.

questions.explanation: The range 25.2 - 24.8 = 0.4 cm3 is used about the mean, so the uncertainty quoted is half of it.
